Learning Objectives
Review the epidemiology and etiology of upper-limb deficiencies.
Identify the types and classification of upper-limb deficiencies.
Describe an appropriate workup for patients with upper-limb deficiency, including assessment
for additional anomalies, general surgical considerations, and prosthetic management.
Overview
Background
Definition: partial or complete absence of the upper extremity that may be unilateral or
bilateral
Varies drastically in presentation, including the affected anatomy and etiology

Poses unique challenges in pediatric patients because of their skeletal immaturity, growth,
and family involvement
Epidemiology
Incidence varies with etiology.
Congenital Limb Deficiencies
Variability in reporting cases and gene pools worldwide makes obtaining precise numbers a
challenge.
In the United States, no formal complete registry of birth differences exists.1,2
Approximately 5 in 10,000 live births or approximately 1,500 to 2,500 infants per year affected
in the United States3
Ratio of upper to lower extremity involvement is 3:1.4
Account for approximately 60% of children treated in pediatric amputee clinics, including
upper and lower extremity congenital limb loss5
Acquired Limb Deficiencies: Approximately 40% of acquired amputations involve the upper
extremity.5

Congenital Limb Deficiencies
A large retrospective study collected data on amputation injuries in pediatric patients
using the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System between 1990 and 2002. This
study was the first to assess the demographics of a national sample of children with
traumatic amputations. Approximately 111,600 children younger than 18 years
presented to emergency departments in the United States over a 12-year period with
amputation injuries. The mean age of patients who sustained injury was 6.18 years;
65.5% of the patients were male. Of all amputations, 91.6% were finger amputations.6
Etiology
Congenital Deficiencies

Embryology
The first trimester is the most critical time for limb genesis.
The mesoderm forms at approximately day 26 of gestation and continues to differentiate
until 8 weeks of gestation. Limb development occurs proximally to distally under the
influence of various genes.7,8
Risk factors
Associated anomalies
Organogenesis occurs at the same time as mesodermal formation and differentiation,
making associated anomalies more prevalent in children with upper extremity differences
than in those with lower extremity differences.9
Such syndromes generally result in bilateral deficiencies and are critical to diagnose because
of their potentially life-threatening associated conditions.
The most high-yield examples of associated syndromes Include the following:
Thrombocytopenia with absence of radius (TAR) syndrome: Preserved mildly hypoplastic
thumbs
Fanconi anemia
Anemia and leukopenia by age 5 to 6 years
Hypoplastic or absent thumb, first metacarpal, or radius
Holt-Oram syndrome
Congenital heart disease, most commonly atrial septal defect and tetralogy of Fallot
Radial longitudinal deficiency, specifically radial dysplasia
Baller-Gerold syndrome
Craniosynostosis
Oligodactyly, malformed or absent thumbs, radial ray malformations, and partial or
complete absence of bones in the forearm
VACTERL association (VATER) syndrome
Acronyms used to describe a series of birth defects that occur together: vertebral defects,
anal atresia, cardiac defects, tracheoesophageal fistula, renal dysplasia, limb deficiency
Radial aplasia, hypoplastic humerus, aplasia in lower limb
Diamond-Blackfan anemia
Bone marrow failure disorder with anemia and reticulocytopenia
Radial longitudinal deficiency
Maternal factors and intrauterine growth
Maternal or gestational diabetes18,19

Tobacco use is associated with an increased risk for digit anomalies.20
Ingestion of certain drugs, such as thalidomide
Vascular disruptions
Amniotic band syndrome involves constriction of limbs or digits by a thin fibrous band of
amniotic tissue and may result in potential amputation. No identified risk factors are
associated with amniotic band formation.22,23
Some examples of syndromes associated with vascular pathology and upper-limb defects
include Adams-Oliver syndrome, Klippel-Feil syndrome, Moebius syndrome, Poland
syndrome, and terminal transverse deficiency.24

Congenital Deficiencies
Children with TAR syndrome commonly present with varying degrees of bilateral radius
abnormalities with mildly hypoplastic thumbs. They also may have additional skeletal
abnormalities involving the lower extremities and the ulna.10 TAR syndrome results from
mutations in the RBM8A gene and has an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.11
Diagnosis of TAR syndrome is critical because of the potential need for blood
transfusions in the setting of thrombocytopenia.12
Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder; at least seven different
genes are implicated. It is characterized by bone marrow failure, resulting in
pancytopenia. A high risk exists for the development of acute leukemia by adulthood.
Associated features may include café au lait spots, microphthalmia, short stature,
microcephaly, developmental delay, renal anomalies, and genitourinary anomalies in
boys. The most common musculoskeletal defects include radial hypoplasia and radial ray
defects, such as hypoplastic thumb. The disorder can be diagnosed via a chromosome
breakage test.13
Holt-Oram syndrome also is referred to as the hand-heart syndrome. The most common
upper-limb malformations include radial hypoplasia or aplasia and fused or abnormal
carpal bones. Regardless of the high association with congenital heart disease, all
patients have an increased risk for cardiac conduction disease. The disease is inherited
in an autosomal dominant manner, with implication of the TBX5 gene.14

Baller-Gerold syndrome should be considered in infants born with premature fusion of
the cranial bones (craniosynostosis), most commonly the coronal suture, in the setting of
an upper-limb deficiency. The most common upper-limb deficiencies include a
hypoplastic or aplastic thumb, radial hypoplasia or aplasia, and malformed or absent
carpal or metacarpal bones. Other manifestations include skin erythema, poikiloderma,
and short stature. The syndrome is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, and the
RECQL4 gene is affected.15
Children with VACTERL syndrome typically have at least three of the described
malformations, with 40% to 50% of patients presenting with limb malformations.
VACTERL is sporadic and must be differentiated from overlapping conditions.16
Diamond-Blackfan anemia is a sporadic, heterogeneous bone marrow disorder that
results in bone marrow dysfunction causing anemia and reticulocytopenia. More than
one-third of patients present with physical malformations, including upper-limb defects.
Additional features may include craniofacial anomalies, urinary or renal system
malformations, heart anomalies, and short stature. Partial phenotypes make diagnosis a
challenge.17
Thalidomide was created in the mid 1950s to manage morning sickness during
pregnancy; however, it was never approved for use in the United States. It was taken off
the market by 1962 because of birth anomalies and, occasionally, infant death.21
Acquired Deficiencies
Trauma
Trauma is the leading cause of acquired upper-limb deficiency.
A single limb is involved in more 90% of patients.25
The lower extremity is affected in approximately 80% of patients.26
The prevalence in boys compared with girls is 3:1.25
The types of trauma vary geographically.
In rural areas, common causes of trauma include lawn mower injuries and high-tension wire
injuries.

Throughout the world, war-zone–related injuries, including landmine explosions, are the
leading cause of acquired amputations in children.27
Trauma also varies with age.
From the ages of 1 to 4 years, power tools and household accidents (specifically involving
doors), are the most common causes of traumatic limb amputation.
Older children are more likely to sustain limb loss from motor vehicle collisions, gunshot
wounds, power tools, and fireworks.
Adolescents tend to have more serious injuries than younger children.25,27
Disease
Disease is the second leading cause of acquired limb deficiency in the pediatric population,
and tumors represent the most common type of disease.25
The most common tumors associated with acquired limb amputations are osteosarcoma,
Ewing sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.
Such tumors have the highest incidence between ages 12 and 21 years.
Infections
Purpura fulminans is a potentially fatal dermatologic emergency caused by multiple bacterial
infections, most commonly Neisseria meningitidis. It results in hemorrhagic necrosis and
thrombosis of the skin. Often, patients who survive are left with multiple amputations. It is
the leading infectious cause of amputation in infants and children.27
Meningococcal disease also may result in septic emboli that may lead to amputations, with
no predilection for the upper versus lower extremities.28
Vascular injuries
Rare cause of amputation, mostly occurring in utero during chorionic villus sampling or
postnatally in infants who require vascular access27,32
Burn injuries
Classified as electrical, chemical, or thermal injuries
They are more common in adults.
Pediatric patients have an increased risk for thermal injuries if preparing meals
unsupervised.
Such injuries can become infected and lead to amputation.26
Frostbite injuries also can be considered in high-latitude regions.26

Acquired Deficiencies
An important consideration in the skeletally immature population is involvement of the
physeal plates. In such patients, surgical epiphysiodesis, in which bone growth at the
physeal plate is temporarily or permanently arrested, may be necessary to correct and
prevent limb deformities.29,30 Such infections also may target the skin, ultimately
requiring skin grafts that may limit the use of a prosthesis.31 Cases of meningococcal
infection are declining because of vaccination.
Types of Upper-Limb Deficiencies
Shoulder Disarticulation and Intrascapulothoracic Deficiencies
Restoration of function is a challenge, especially in patients with bilateral deficiencies.
The child may make several accommodations.
The axilla and parts of the humerus (if applicable) may assist with activities of daily living.
If a unilateral deficiency is present, grasping is performed by the contralateral limb, with
manipulation via various combinations, including the knees, mouth, chin, and chest.25
With bilateral deficiencies, children may depend on the feet to grasp and manipulate objects.25
Because of a lack of glenohumeral flexion, many patients cannot provide the body movement
necessary to control the mechanical components of the prosthesis.25
Transhumeral Deficiencies
The residual limb generally is short to medium in length.
Greatest risk for diaphyseal overgrowth25
Longitudinal Deficiencies of the Humerus
Generally associated with radial and ulnar deficiencies and phocomelic digits (hands are
directly attached to the trunk)
Such associations compromise arm length and pose a challenge to performing bimanual tasks,
making prostheses a viable option.25

Elbow Disarticulation
Partial or complete compromise of the elbow joint may increase dependence on the muscles
and range of motion of the shoulder complex to preserve function25 (Figure 1).
The distal epiphysis is preserved in patients with a true elbow disarticulation.25
Figure 1 AP radiograph demonstrates a complete elbow disarticulation. (Reproduced from Cho

Prosthetic, and Rehabilitation Principles, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2016, pp 249-255.)
Transverse Deficiencies of the Forearm
The most common upper-limb deficiency is at the level of the upper one-third of the
forearm25 (Figure 2).
The proximal radius generally is unstable and can experience anterior subluxation during
extension, thereby limiting the available amount of contact with the prosthesis.25
For longer residual limbs (spanning the middle one-third or more), more surface area is
available, making it is easier to fit and control a prosthesis.25

If prostheses are not used, patients rely on the cubital fold, legs, axillary region, or chin to

Longitudinal Deficiencies of the Forearm
The two most common longitudinal deficiencies are radial and ulnar deficiencies.33
Phocomelia, the third type of longitudinal deficiency, is rarer and may represent a severe
manifestation of radial and/or ulnar deficiency.
Radial deficiencies are 5 to 10 times more prevalent than ulnar deficiencies.25
Radial deficiencies (Figure 3)

Radial-sided digits, including the thumb, usually also are hypoplastic or absent.33
The degree of thumb deficiency correlates with the severity of the radial deficiency.33
The index and long fingers may be stiff; however, the ring and little fingers usually are

The wrist is unstable because of lack of radial support.33
A combination of finger abnormalities and wrist instability leads to weak grip.33
Such patients may need to rely on their toes for transfers.33

Associated with TAR, Fanconi anemia, VACTERL, Holt-Oram syndrome, and thalidomide
use25,33

Typically present unilaterally
The ulna is partially or completely absent, with a shortened or bowed radius.33

Classification of Upper-Limb Deficiency
Varies based on the etiology of the deficiency
Congenital Deficiency
Classic classification
Described by ancient language roots
Terminology includes a combination of the following word parts: “a” for absent, “hemi” for
half, “melia” for limb, “mero” for partial, “dactyly” for metacarpal/metatarsal, “phalang” for
digit, and “chiria” for hand.34
International Society for Prosthetics and Orthotics (ISPO) classification
Categorizes limb deficiency on anatomic and radiologic basis
ISPO was created to reduce the ambiguity occasionally associated with the classic
classification system.35
The limb is classified as a transverse or longitudinal deficiency.
Transverse deficiencies are named for the last segment of the limb that is present, and no
portions are preserved distal to the level name.36,37 For example, according to the ISPO

Longitudinal deficiencies have portions distal to the level and are named for the affected
bones.36,37
Frantz-O’Rahilly classification
Classifies deficiencies as terminal or intercalary, with subclassification into horizontal and
longitudinal defects25,37
Terminal refers to complete loss of the distal extremity.25,37
Intercalary refers to the absence of intermediate parts of the extremity, with preservation of
proximal and distal components.25,37
Acquired Deficiency
Classified in a manner similar to adult limb loss
Examples include intrascapulothoracic, shoulder disarticulation, transhumeral (above the
elbow), elbow disarticulation, transradial (below the elbow), wrist disarticulation, and partial
hand amputation.38
Clinical Presentation
Patient History and Physical Examination
Congenital limb loss is associated with digital deficiencies more commonly than long bone
deficiencies and with longitudinal defects more commonly than transverse defects.39
If congenital limb loss is diagnosed, a thorough patient history and physical examination,
including a detailed family history, must be performed to detect potentially associated
anomalies.
Additional imaging studies, such as a renal ultrasonography, skeletal survey, and
echocardiography, may be necessary.
For patients with a radial deficiency, a complete blood count with differential should be
obtained to assess for bone marrow dysfunction.10
Children with upper-limb deficiencies have an increased risk for certain medical conditions,
particularly scoliosis, congenital and idiopathic.40,41
Bracing is a challenge in children with an upper-limb prosthesis.

Scoliosis generally is progressive in this patient population and may warrant surgical
management.
The patient’s function should be considered postoperatively because range of motion may be
limited at the lower extremities, which may affect function.42-44
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs highlight the affected anatomy.
MRI and CT may be performed for more complex cases or surgical planning.
Management
General Approach
Most effectively managed via a multidisciplinary approach
Each child presents unique challenges.
Treatment of children with upper-limb deficiency varies with etiology, expected skeletal
maturity, and psychosocial factors.
Some children require surgical treatment in addition to prosthetic management, whereas
other children do not require treatment.
Surgical approach for acquired upper-limb loss
General Principles
The potential growth in skeletally immature patients further complicates their treatment and
must be considered before any management.
Each bone grows at a different rate and in a different manner. For example, for every 10 mm
in growth at the humerus, 8 mm of growth occurs proximally and 2 mm occurs distally. The
opposite is true for the radius, with most growth occurring distally.27
Some general principles to consider include:
Preservation of limb length45
Preservation of growth plates45
Preference for disarticulation versus transosseous amputation45

Stabilize and normalize the proximal aspect of the residual limb.45
Proper surgical management enables optimal prosthetic use in the future.
Etiology of the limb loss guides surgicl management.
Because of improved detection and management, most tumors are managed via limb salvage
rather than amputation.25,27
For traumatic injuries, amputations may be performed immediately in patients with severe
hemorrhage or critical ischemia (>6 hours) or for incomplete traumatic amputations.26
Amputations may be reserved for later in patients in whom pressing issues require
management.
Infectious etiologies of upper-limb deficiency require clear delineation of pathologic versus
healthy bone, which can be determined via technetium Tc 99m bone scintigraphy.
Amputations are not performed until the extent of dry gangrene is finalized, apart from life-
threatening, wet gangrene.26
Burn patients undergo limited limb salvage procedures because of the damage to the
overlying soft tissue.26

General Principles
Commonly, disarticulations are preferred over transosseous amputations for several
reasons. Disarticulations preserve the epiphyseal growth plates, thereby allowing for
longitudinal growth. Disarticulations also are associated less likely to result in terminal
bony overgrowth;46 however, disarticulations may pose a challenge to prosthetists
because of the length of the residual limb.
Limb salvage procedures involve the removal and replacement of the diseased bone
with a metal endoprosthesis. The procedure may be selected because of its limb
preservation and improved cosmesis but ultimately depends on the stage and
responsiveness of the cancer to neoadjuvant therapy and the ability to attain tumor-free
margins of 5 to 8 cm. In patients with osteosarcoma, as many as 90% of patients may be
offered this procedure over traditional limb amputation.25,27 The rates of recurrence
and long-term survival are similar between limb salvage procedures and amputations.26
The functionality of the affected limb is the key element in determining function and
quality of life in these patients.47-50 Therefore, options should be discussed with patients

oncologists, and physiatrists/pediatric rehabilitation medicine physicians.
The types of limb salvage procedures available include local tissue flaps, transfers, or
excisions; autologous transfers; allograft transplantation; endoprostheses; intercalary
resections; and bone transfers.26
Relative contraindications to limb salvage are pathologic fracture, surgical site infection,
predicted limb-length discrepancy greater than 8 to 10 cm, substantial soft-tissue
involvement, a poor response to chemotherapy preoperatively, or vascular invasion by
the tumor that poses a sizeable challenge to vascular reconstruction.26
Wound Coverage and Incision Closure
Tissue viability is better in children than in adults.
Wound coverage is more easily achieved in pediatric patients.
Prosthetic Management
Purpose
Optimize function and independence
Assist with social acceptance
More useful for specific tasks than for daily function
Encourage bimanual tasks; improve efficiency with manual tasks.51
Allow for symmetric crawling
Does not guarantee acceptance of the prosthesis but may encourage wearing habits52
Achieve age-appropriate milestones; children with upper-limb deficiencies achieve
milestones at approximately the same age as those without limb deficiencies.25
Data on upper-limb prostheses are conflicting because some studies do not demonstrate
improved function and quality of life, whereas other studies demonstrate improved function
with early prosthetic fitting.

Prosthetic Management
A multicenter study assessed quality of life and function in 489 children with unilateral
congenital below-elbow deficiency. Of the 489 children, 321 wore a prosthesis, and 168
did not wear a prosthesis. Several outcome measures were used, including the Pediatric
Outcomes Data Collection Instrument, the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory, the
Prosthetic Upper Extremity Functional Index, and the Unilateral Below Elbow Test. The
Pediatric Outcomes Data Collection Instrument and the Pediatric Quality of Life
Inventory scores did not demonstrate any clinically relevant differences between the two
groups of patients. The Unilateral Below Elbow Test scores were relatively the same in
both groups. Compared with the general population, the Pediatric Quality of Life
Inventory scores were relatively the same for children with unilateral below-elbow
deficiencies. Overall, the study showed little improvement in function or quality of life
with a prosthesis.51
A retrospective case series of 260 patients was conducted to assess experiences with
prosthetic management, including determining the optimal age for prosthetic fitting, the
optimal prosthetic design, and the appropriate level of prosthetic training. The study
showed considerable improvement in prosthetic outcome in patients fit before age 3
years but no additional benefit in those fit before age 1 year.53
Evaluation for a Prosthesis
Increased family involvement in the decision-making process
Children rely on parents or loved ones for appointments and prosthetic care.
Devise an age-appropriate explanation for the child’s limb loss that they can use among their
peers.
Educate parents on the etiology of the limb loss.
Assessment of the family’s and the child’s motivation and commitment to a prosthesis is
critical for successful prosthetic wear.54
If parents accept a prosthesis, they are more likely to encourage their child to comply with
wearing the device.25

Discuss the options for a prosthesis and the advantages and complications.
Children with congenital limb deficiency generally accept their deficiency more readily than
their parents, family, and friends. Children may not see the need for a prosthesis, but their
family and friends may insist.
Children with congenital upper-limb loss are less likely to use a prosthesis than those with
acquired limb loss because trauma typically occurs later in childhood in the latter group.
Children with congenital limb loss already learned the appropriate adaptations.
The higher the deficiency, the less likely the child is to wear the prosthesis. Transradial
deficiency has greater compliance than transhumeral deficiency, which has greater compliance
than shoulder disarticulation.55
Clearly identify the child’s and the family’s goals for a prosthesis.
Recognize that the goals for prosthetic fitting are dynamic as children progress through
milestones and growth.25
Parents may push for a prosthesis as a method of coping with their child’s deficiency and may
need to see the child reject the prosthesis to accept the limb loss.
Types of Prostheses
Upper-Limb Body-Powered Prostheses
General
Most commonly prescribed upper-limb prosthesis56
Operation
Relies on body movements and a cable system (occasionally referred to as cable-driven
prostheses)57
Advantages
Inexpensive
Lightweight
Reliable
Increased level of proprioception
Durable (can be used in various climates)
Simplistic mechanics
Disadvantages
Substantial force and effort may be necessary to power the device. Individuals with high-level
limb loss may not have the necessary power.57

The terminal device is the most distal part of the prosthesis.
Terminal device substitutes hand function.

Prosthetic Complications
Terminal bony overgrowth at the distal end of the residual limb is the most common
complication after amputation in skeletally immature children. It typically results in a
pointed end at the residual limb that may irritate the overlying soft tissue, potentially
resulting in ulcerations through the skin.83 This process may lead to multiple
complications, including poor prosthetic fit and tolerance. The most commonly affected
bone is the humerus, followed by the lower extremity bones.38 It is the leading cause of
surgical revision in children with an amputation.27 Examples of the types of surgical
revision procedures performed include osteotomies and endoprosthetic caps to occlude
the terminal end of the bone.84 Surgical revision may pose a challenge for prosthetic fit
because with each bone resection, the ability to control the prosthesis is reduced.
Unfortunately, surgical management is not a permanent solution, and the problem
tends to recur until skeletal maturity is achieved.25
Prosthesis Rejection
Prostheses are readily rejected by children because of the previously described complications.
Lack of sensory feedback, in which a patient with limb deficiency is missing a representation of
the deficient limb in their brain, also plays a role.86
Without prostheses, children with upper-limb differences generally have nearly normal
function and quality of life.

Congenital differences are the leading cause of upper-limb loss in pediatrics.
Congenital upper-limb malformations may be associated with other congenital anomalies;
therefore, a thorough patient history and physical examination are important because some
conditions may be life-threatening.
